scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): grants that outside forces shape behaviour, then argues personal choice still matters; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: We are all born into a family, a place, and a time that we did not choose.
Some people claim that people's behaviour is largely determined by forces not of their own making.
I agree that outside forces shape us powerfully, but I believe our own choices still play a vital part.

sections.role: Body 1 — How outside forces shape us

sentences.text: First, much of our behaviour really is shaped by forces beyond our control.
Our family, culture, and upbringing teach us how to act long before we can choose for ourselves.
For example, a child raised amid violence may grow up treating aggression as normal.
This shows that circumstances can deeply influence how a person comes to behave.
Poverty, education, and the people around us all push our behaviour in powerful directions.
Even our genes and health can shape our moods and choices in ways we never decided.
To this extent, the claim points to a real and important truth.
Second, however, our own choices still shape our behaviour in crucial ways.
People raised in the very same hard conditions often make strikingly different choices.
Consider two children from the same troubled home, where one turns to crime and the other to helping others.
Such differences show that human beings are not simply puppets of their circumstances.
We can reflect on our situation, resist bad influences, and decide to change our path.
Holding people responsible for their actions only makes sense because they truly can choose.
Free choice, then, works alongside outside forces rather than being erased by them.
In conclusion, forces beyond our control do shape much of our behaviour.
But our own choices still matter, since people in the same conditions often act very differently.
Our behaviour is best understood as the meeting of outside forces and personal choice.
